name: Cervical Facet Joint Syndrome
description: Facet-mediated cervical pain provoked by extension and ipsilateral rotation. Affects cervical motion segments and surrounding cervicoscapular musculature. Typical presentation includes localised pain reproduced by mechanical loading or specific positions, with reproducible findings on physical examination. Phase-based PT: modulate symptoms, restore mobility and motor control, then graded loading and return to function.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with cervical facet joint syndrome on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

etiology: Multifactorial: load, capacity and individual risk factors interact in Cervical Facet Joint Syndrome.
epidemiology: Cervical musculoskeletal presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Pathology localised to the joint of the cervical region, with characteristic findings on examination and (where indicated) imaging.
clinical_presentation: Facet-mediated cervical pain provoked by extension and ipsilateral rotation.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.
mechanism: Mechanical overload (repetitive microtrauma or single-event force) exceeds tissue capacity in the cervical region, producing local nociceptive input and protective motor responses.
anatomy: Seven cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) form a lordotic curve. C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) provide ~50% of cervical rotation. Facet joints orient ~45° in lower segments allowing flexion/extension and rotation. Stabilised by deep cervical flexors (longus colli/capitis), suboccipitals, scalenes, SCM and posterior cervical extensors. Neural structures: spinal cord, exiting nerve roots C1–C8 and the vertebral artery passing through transverse foramina C6–C1.

anatomy: Glenohumeral joint is a shallow ball-and-socket relying on the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), labrum and capsuloligamentous complex. Scapulothoracic articulation, AC and SC joints contribute to ~60° scapular rotation during arm elevation (scapulohumeral rhythm). Subacromial space contains supraspinatus tendon, long head of biceps and subacromial bursa.

name: Multidirectional Instability
description: Symptomatic instability in ≥2 directions. Affects the glenohumeral joint, rotator cuff and scapulothoracic complex. Typical presentation includes localised pain reproduced by mechanical loading or specific positions, with reproducible findings on physical examination. Phase-based PT: modulate symptoms, restore mobility and motor control, then graded loading and return to function.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with multidirectional instability on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

epidemiology: Knee sports presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Cortical and/or trabecular bone failure; classification by location, pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted), displacement and articular involvement.
clinical_presentation: Stress fracture of tibia in runners.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.

mechanism: Bone fails when applied load exceeds its strength — high-energy trauma, repetitive submaximal loading (stress fracture) or pathological weakening (osteoporosis, tumour).
anatomy: Modified hinge: tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints. Static stabilisers: ACL/PCL, MCL/LCL, menisci, capsule. Dynamic stabilisers: quadriceps (especially VMO for patellar tracking), hamstrings, popliteus, gastrocnemius. Q-angle and patellofemoral alignment influence patellar tracking and load distribution.

Typical presentation includes localised pain reproduced by mechanical loading or specific positions, with reproducible findings on physical examination. Phase-based PT: modulate symptoms, restore mobility and motor control, then graded loading and return to function.
key_findings: Clinical findings consistent with spondylolisthesis (isthmic) — acute stage on history and physical examination.
diagnostic_tips: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging only when red flags are present or if it will change management.

treatment_plan.acute: Protect tissue; modulate pain (manual therapy, modalities as adjunct); patient education on load management.
treatment_plan.subacute: Restore ROM and motor control; introduce graded isometric/isotonic loading specific to involved tissue.
treatment_plan.chronic: Progressive resistance, capacity building and functional/sport-specific loading aligned with patient goals.

etiology: Multifactorial: load, capacity and individual risk factors interact in Spondylolisthesis (Isthmic) — Acute Stage.
epidemiology: Lumbar musculoskeletal presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Pathology localised to the bone of the lumbar region, with characteristic findings on examination and (where indicated) imaging.
clinical_presentation: Anterior slippage secondary to pars defect. Presentation in the acute stage of healing/adaptation.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.
mechanism: Repetitive lumbar extension-rotation (e.g. fast bowling, gymnastics) creates pars interarticularis stress fracture; bilateral defects allow anterior vertebral translation.
anatomy: Five lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5) form a lordotic curve over the sacrum. Sagittally oriented facets favour flexion/extension and limit rotation. Intervertebral discs (anulus fibrosus + nucleus pulposus) bear axial load. Stabilised by multifidus, transversus abdominis, erector spinae, quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia. Cauda equina contains L2–S5 nerve roots.

pathophysiology: Tendinopathic continuum (Cook & Purdam): reactive tendinopathy → tendon dysrepair → degenerative tendinopathy. Histology shows collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, neovascularisation and absence of classic inflammatory infiltrate.
clinical_presentation: Lateral ankle tendinopathy. Presentation in the acute stage of healing/adaptation.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.
mechanism: Mechanical overload (repetitive microtrauma or single-event force) exceeds tissue capacity in the foot/ankle region, producing local nociceptive input and protective motor responses.
anatomy: Talocrural (mortise) joint provides dorsiflexion/plantarflexion; subtalar joint controls inversion/eversion. Lateral ligament complex (ATFL > CFL > PTFL) most commonly injured. Plantar fascia, intrinsic foot muscles and three arches (medial/lateral longitudinal, transverse) support load transfer. Gastroc-soleus complex inserts via Achilles tendon.

mechanism: Mechanical overload (repetitive microtrauma or single-event force) exceeds tissue capacity in the cervical region, producing local nociceptive input and protective motor responses.
anatomy: Seven cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) form a lordotic curve. C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) provide ~50% of cervical rotation. Facet joints orient ~45° in lower segments allowing flexion/extension and rotation. Stabilised by deep cervical flexors (longus colli/capitis), suboccipitals, scalenes, SCM and posterior cervical extensors. Neural structures: spinal cord, exiting nerve roots C1–C8 and the vertebral artery passing through transverse foramina C6–C1.

MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed

etiology: Multifactorial: load, capacity and individual risk factors interact in Achilles Tendinopathy (Mid-portion) — Subacute Stage.
epidemiology: Foot/Ankle musculoskeletal presentation commonly seen in physiotherapy practice.
pathophysiology: Tendinopathic continuum (Cook & Purdam): reactive tendinopathy → tendon dysrepair → degenerative tendinopathy. Histology shows collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, neovascularisation and absence of classic inflammatory infiltrate.
clinical_presentation: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. Presentation in the subacute stage of healing/adaptation.
imaging: Plain radiograph if indicated
MRI/US for soft-tissue characterization when needed
prognosis: Generally favourable with appropriate, progressive rehabilitation.
return_to_activity: Criterion-based: pain control, ROM, strength symmetry and functional performance.
mechanism: Repetitive eccentric loading and accumulated load above tendon capacity produce mid-portion or insertional tendinopathy with collagen disorganisation and neovascularisation.
anatomy: Talocrural (mortise) joint provides dorsiflexion/plantarflexion; subtalar joint controls inversion/eversion. Lateral ligament complex (ATFL > CFL > PTFL) most commonly injured. Plantar fascia, intrinsic foot muscles and three arches (medial/lateral longitudinal, transverse) support load transfer. Gastroc-soleus complex inserts via Achilles tendon.
